newsitem.title: UK: RTRS-London gold market to loosen veil of secrecy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-London gold market to loosen veil of secrecy.

text.p: A veil of secrecy which has cloaked dealings in bullion for centuries is about to be lifted a little.

But the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), which says it will announce new measures to make the world trade in precious metals more transparent on Wednesday, is, true to form, being canny right to the end about what exactly these are.
"I am not prepared to say anything until we make an announcement," said LBMA chairman Allan Baker.
Some idea of the scale of the market is already public.

At a conference in late 1995 Bank of England official Terry Smeeton revealed that turnover in the London gold market averaged 250 tonnes daily which was significantly more than any of the other centres such as in New York, Tokyo or Zurich.
Based on a 250-day working year, that would make London gold trade turnover 62,500 tonnes a year.
The authoritative research group Gold Field Mineral Services estimate new mine production of gold at 2,328 tonnes in 1996.
Most market participants welcomed the move to bring a little more light to a trade in which London has been pre-eminent for centuries.
But Tony Warwick-Ching a gold market research consultant at CRU International said, "I'm a bit schizoid about it. On the one hand I am delighted that more information will be released to the world.
"But it is not clear why it is of commercial interest to publish more. Other markets publish a lot more and are not necessarily trouble free," he said.
According to LBMA chairman Baker, international settlement and London market turnover figures for the final quarter of 1996 will be issued on Wednesday with the cooperation of the Bank of England.
A central bank spokesman said, "We welcome this initiative which came from the LBMA."
Baker confirmed the move was in response to calls from international market participants for greater transparency.
"We will be announcing statistics that will reflect the magnitude of the market," he said. "One is not giving anything away but at the same time one is trying to put some dimension to it.'
One indicator which some market observers would like to see is the turnover on the twice-daily gold fixing.

"The area where you always get secrecy was turnover at the fixing. That would be a much better measure of the market (than announcing daily turnover totalled in billions of dollars)," one senior market analyst said.
He added, "They (the LBMA) must have a story to tell. People will learn to read things into them like reading things into the leasing rate moving up and down and open interest data from Comex."
Transactions in gold have not always been conducted in secret.

As European embarked on a period of maritime expansion they were anything but secretive in grabbing the gold hoards of older but less robust civilisations. Gold helped create ostentatious fortunes built of the European Renaissance and to finance the Industrial Revolution - and countless wars.

As world trade in the metal matured so its centre moved to London where an established financial infrastructure smoothed transactions. The development of the South African gold fields cemented London's position.
But gold's increasing commercial role led inexorably to greater stealth in conducting business.

Rhona O'Connell, metals markets analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co, said the market could benefit from releasing information at a time when the gold price was recovering from a slump which had token it down four percent to a 40-month low this year.
"It could show potential investors that the market is deeper and more liquid than they would otherwise have thought if all they saw is the price going down," she said.
